title: Pan-Seared Fish
ingredients: 2 skinless tilefish or other sturdy, thick white fish fillets (about 7 to 8 ounces each), skins removed
3 green garlic shoots or scallions, thinly sliced
1 1/2 tablespoons tablespoons finely chopped chives, mint, lovage and/or sorrel
1 tablespoon minced lemon thyme or regular leaves
2 teaspoons finely chopped tarragon, basil or marjoram
directions: Remove any remaining pin bones in the fish, pat dry, and season both sides with salt and pepper.

In a large sauté pan over medium heat, melt butter. Once butter has begun to foam, lay fish in pan. Add green garlic or scallions and a pinch of salt. Without disturbing the fish, tilt the pan toward you; using a spoon, ladle green garlic butter over fish. Continue basting fish for 2 to 3 minutes.
Using a spatula, gently flip fish. Reduce heat to low, cover pan and cook for 2 minutes.
Uncover pan, add herbs and continue basting fish with butter until it is just cooked through, another minute or two longer.
Transfer fish to a serving platter or individual plates, pour pan sauce over the top, and pour lemon juice over everything. Season with more salt and black pepper if needed. Serve immediately.

All cooks need a basic sautéed fish fillet recipe in their repertory, and this is mine. Or, at least, this is a version of mine. Since I almost never make the exact same dish twice, this recipe narrates the basic technique. The ingredients themselves vary ad infinitum.

The method could not be much simpler, but it does involve one important step: basting the fish with the fat you’re cooking it in. To do this, you’ll need to use a good amount of fat, about a tablespoon per person (you could get away with a little less if you insist, or use half white wine and half fat). Basting helps cook the fish evenly and keeps it nice and moist.

In this recipe, I use butter as the fat. As the fish cooks, the butter browns, taking on a nutty scent that is classic with seafood. Olive oil, peanut oil, coconut oil, even lard would work as a substitute, though without the creaminess of butter.

Another important point here is to handle the fish as little as possible. Fillets are delicate; moving them around too much will break them up. So flip them once, and don’t poke them. I love to use green garlic with fish, but if you can’t find it, substitute scallions. If you love garlic, you can throw in a minced clove along with the herbs.
Any thick, white fish fillets will work here: tilefish, cod, halibut, blackfish. Thin fillets, like porgy or flounder, will also work, though they will cook a little more quickly.

And, of course, use whatever herbs you have around. In spring, I made this with sorrel. Now that summer’s at hand, mint, basil and oregano can step in. And if you save this recipe for winter, sturdy Italian parsley substitutes nicely for all the herbs. In this case though, use plenty of garlic — which is, after all, good advice with fish in general.
